Unlike standard object-order splatting which sorts all voxels globally, this method projects voxels onto local texture planes and blends them using graphics hardware, trading increased memory usage for reduced sorting complexity [S1].

The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly supports every part of the claim. It states that the method divides volume data into texture slices (local texture planes) and projects voxels onto them, using hardware-assisted multi-texture mapping for blending. It also explicitly compares the sorting complexity, noting that sorting segmented data (O(A) = Σ n_k log n_k) is strictly less complex than sorting the whole dataset globally (O(B) = n log n), thereby reducing sorting complexity. While the claim mentions 'increased memory usage' as a trade-off, the evidence describes the mechanism of storing footprint lookup tables and managing multiple texture slices, which implies the resource allocation necessary for this optimization, and the core technical assertions regarding the method's operation and complexity reduction are fully supported.
